```powershell
cd C:\Users\sh3qm\code\ibis_comparison

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

# Stop the earlier too-large overnight run, but only if that exact command is still running.
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
  Where-Object {
    $_.CommandLine -like "*run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py*" -and
    $_.CommandLine -like "*sparam_vector_fit_campaign_v1_2026-06-17_overnight*"
  } |
  ForEach-Object {
    Write-Host "Stopping old run PID $($_.ProcessId)"
    Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force
  }

$StudyDir = "results\sparam_vector_fit_campaign_v1_2026-06-17_fast_overnight"
$Ngspice = "\\minerfiles.mst.edu\dfs\users\sh3qm\Downloads\ngspice-46_64\Spice64\bin\ngspice_con.exe"

$ExtraTouchstone = "hspice\sparam"

foreach ($Path in @($Ngspice, $Hspice, $SkrfTarget, $SkrfTests, $ExtraTouchstone)) {
  if (!(Test-Path $Path)) {
    throw "Missing required path: $Path"
  }
}

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$StudyDir\logs" | Out-Null

function Run-Step {
  param(
    [string]$Name,
    [string]$Log,
    [string[]]$Args
  )

  Write-Host ""
  Write-Host "========== $Name =========="
  Write-Host "Log: $Log"
  & py -3.14 -u @Args 2>&1 | Tee-Object -FilePath $Log
  if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
    throw "$Name failed with exit code $LASTEXITCODE"
  }
}

Run-Step `
  -Name "01 vector-fit pilot fitting" `
  -Log "$StudyDir\logs\01_fit.log" `
  -Args @(
    "scripts/run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py", "fit",
    "--study-dir", $StudyDir,
    "--skrf-target", $SkrfTarget,
    "--skrf-tests-dir", $SkrfTests,
    "--extra-touchstone-dir", $ExtraTouchstone,
    "--candidate-profile", "pilot",
    "--preprocess", "raw,dc_hold",
    "--dense-samples", "201",
    "--max-channels", "40"
  )

Run-Step `
  -Name "02 ngspice smoke" `
  -Log "$StudyDir\logs\02_smoke_ngspice.log" `
  -Args @(
    "scripts/run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py", "smoke-ngspice",
    "--study-dir", $StudyDir,

  )

Run-Step `

    "--sim-timeout", "240",
    "--audit-stop-ns", "35",
    "--max-channels", "20",
    "--resume"
  )

Run-Step `

  -Log "$StudyDir\logs\04_report.log" `

  )

Write-Host ""
Write-Host "DONE. Main report:"
```

```powershell
Run-Step `

Write-Host ""
Write-Host "DONE. Main report:"
```

This is not a scikit-rf failure. It is a PowerShell wrapper issue: the warning is harmless enough, but `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` makes Windows PowerShell stop when Python writes a warning to stderr.

> good so what do we really know and what to really try next?

What we really know:

1. **Vector fitting is not dead.**
   It produced real ngspice `.sp` models, and some matched HSPICE well.
2. **But it is not generally trustworthy yet.**
   In the 40-channel pilot, independent selection gave:

```text
WARN: 4
FAIL: 36
PASS: 0
```

That is conservative, which is good. We did not accidentally claim anything was fully ready.

3. **HSPICE audit after the fix is clean:**

```text
PASS: 10
WARN: 4
FAIL: 4
ERROR: 0
```

So the audit infrastructure now works.

4. **Edge rate is the big separator.**
   `ntwk2` / `ntwk3` cases generally match HSPICE at `50 ps` and `500 ps`, but become WARN at `5 ps`.

   Clarity is worse:

```text
5 ps:   FAIL
50 ps:  FAIL
500 ps: PASS
```

So vector fitting can look acceptable for slower edges but still fail fast-edge transient behavior.

5. **`raw` preprocessing worked better than `dc_hold`.**
   In this pilot, selected models all came from `raw`. `dc_hold` produced many WARN/FAIL rows and no selected models.
6. **Passivity enforcement did not help enough yet.**
   Enforced variants were generated, but none were selected. Also, scikit-rf warned that some enforcement cases need huge sample counts. So enforcement is not ready as a blind default.
7. **Reduced RX models are still useful, but scoped.**
   They are better for RX-through behavior in some channels, especially Cisco-style `.s4p`, but they are not full multiport replacements. Vector fitting is the better path for a true full-model goal, but it needs more work.

What I would really try next:

1. **Add per-candidate timeout/checkpointing to vector fitting.**
   The full run got stuck because one candidate can take forever. Before another large campaign, we need safe timeouts so a bad fit gets marked `TIMEOUT` and the campaign keeps moving.
2. **Run a focused vector-fit grid, not the giant one.**
   Based on the pilot, start with:

```text
preprocess: raw
orders: 3r3c, 5r5c, 8r8c
spacing: lin/log
passivity enforcement: off initially
```

Then only try passivity enforcement on near-pass models.

3. **Diagnose Clarity specifically.**
   It is the best demo failure case: vector-fit passes at 500 ps but fails at 5/50 ps. We should compare:

```text
Touchstone S21 phase/group delay
vector-fit S21 phase/group delay
Touchstone-derived step response
ngspice vector-fit step response
HSPICE native S-element response
```

That will show whether the failure is delay, high-frequency loss, ringing, causality/pre-response, or extrapolation.

4. **Try better frequency extension/extrapolation.**
   Fast edges need bandwidth beyond the measured data. We should test controlled preprocessing:

```text
DC extrapolation
high-frequency rolloff extension
causal windowing / time-domain gating
trim vs no-trim
```

Not just `dc_hold`.

5. **Compare three model paths side-by-side on the same cases.**

```text
A. scikit-rf vector-fit full model
B. reduced RX-through model
C. BBS / Broadband SPICE model
```

For Clarity, ntwk2/ntwk3, and Cisco channels. That gives a very clear story: which approach helps which failure mode.

6. **Use the current share pack for presentation.**
   It already shows the core finding visually: vector-fit quality varies by channel and edge rate. Next results should explain *why* those differences happen and whether preprocessing/model settings can fix them.

> this is good. push further for the scikit-rf vector fitting method. test more thoroughly, try every tuning/configuration possible, so that we can really build a pipeline: sNp-SPICE, validated through HSPICE correlation and our own metrics. Make a best possible plan.

> Plan
>
> # scikit-rf Vector-Fit S-parameter-to-SPICE Qualification Campaign
>
> ## Summary
>
> Build a robust, resumable campaign that pushes the scikit-rf `VectorFitting` path as far as practical for `sNp -> ngspice .sp` generation. The pipeline will sweep vector-fit configurations, preprocess variants, passivity strategies, and ngspice/HSPICE validation cases, then produce a clear answer: which settings can become a trustworthy full-model workflow, which are only edge-rate/channel-specific, and which fail.
>
> Core rule: HSPICE is used only for correlation/calibration. Normal model selection must be based on independent metrics plus ngspice smoke tests.
>
> ## Key Implementation Changes
>
> - Extend `scripts/run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py` into a staged, resumable campaign runner:
>
>   - Add per-candidate timeout and mark `TIMEOUT` instead of hanging.
>   - Write candidate results incrementally after every fit/export/evaluation.
>   - Add `--resume`, `--workers`, `--candidate-timeout-s`, `--phase-profile`, and `--audit-top-k`.
>   - Keep the recent HSPICE local Touchstone copy fix for all audits.
> - Expand candidate grid beyond the current pilot/full profiles:
>
>   - Fixed fits: `1r1c`, `2r2c`, `3r3c`, `4r4c`, `5r5c`, `6r6c`, `8r8c`, `10r10c`, `12r12c`, `16r16c`, `20r20c`.
>   - Complex-dominant fits: `0r2c`, `0r4c`, `1r3c`, `2r6c`, `4r8c`, `6r12c`.
>   - Sweep `init_pole_spacing=lin,log`, `fit_constant=True,False`, `enforce_dc=True,False`.
>   - Keep `fit_proportional=False` for selectable models; optionally evaluate `True` as diagnostic-only because it can create high-frequency instability.
>   - Auto-fit sweep using scikit-rf knobs: `n_poles_init_real/cmplx`, `n_poles_add`, `model_order_max`, `iters_start/inter/final`, `target_error`, `alpha`, `gamma`, and `nu_samples`.
> - Add preprocessing profiles:
>
>   - Existing: `raw`, `dc_hold`, `freq_trim_0p9`, `freq_trim_0p75`.
>   - New: `freq_trim_0p95`, `freq_trim_0p5`, `linear_resample`, `log_resample`, `lowfreq_dense`, `highfreq_dense`.
>   - New diagnostic high-frequency extensions: `hf_hold`, `hf_rolloff_20db_dec`, `hf_rolloff_40db_dec`.
>   - All candidates must still be scored on the original Touchstone frequency grid.
> - Add passivity strategy sweep:
>

> ## Campaign Phases
>
> - Phase 0: Regression sanity
>
>   - Run only known cases: `Clarity_example`, `Clarity_example_Fitted`, `ntwk2`, `ntwk3`, one Cisco `.s4p`, Molex `.s4p`.
>   - Goal: verify timeout/resume, local HSPICE Touchstone copy, side overlays, and share-pack output.
> - Phase 1: Focused scikit-rf sweep
>
>   - Dataset: same representative cases.
>   - Grid: broad fixed/auto/preprocess/passivity sweep.
>   - Output: best candidate per channel and top 3 HSPICE-audited candidates.
>   - Goal: identify promising settings and eliminate bad settings.
> - Phase 2: Cisco + repo-local calibration
>
>   - Dataset: all Cisco/repo-local `.s2p`/`.s4p`.
>   - Grid: top settings from Phase 1 plus a small exploration tail.
>   - HSPICE audit: selected model plus top 3 candidates for at least 40 channels.
>   - Goal: measure whether independent metrics predict HSPICE correlation by source family and edge rate.
> - Phase 3: Full available dataset
>
>   - Dataset: repo-local, Cisco, Molex, scikit-rf fixtures, and future `--extra-touchstone-dir`.
>   - Grid: only settings that survived Phase 1/2.
>   - Goal: final calibration report with false-pass rate, pass/warn/fail breakdowns, and recommended production defaults.
>
> ## Outputs
>
> - `vf_candidate_grid.csv`: exact candidate settings.
> - `vf_metrics.csv`: independent metrics for every candidate.
> - `vf_ranking.csv`: selected model per channel, independent class, reason.
> - `vf_ngspice_smoke.csv`: ngspice-only transient sanity results.
> - `vf_hspice_correlation.csv`: HSPICE audit rows for selected/top-K candidates.
> - `vf_calibration_summary.csv`: independent class vs HSPICE result, by family/edge/split.
> - `selected_vector_models/`: selected `.sp` models.
> - `plots/`: frequency fit, passivity/singular value, impulse sanity, RX/TX overlays.
> - `share_pack/`: presentation-ready audited cases grouped into `audit_pass`, `audit_warn`, `audit_fail`.
> - `README.md`: headline conclusions, best settings, failure modes, and next recommended defaults.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Unit-style checks:
>
>   - Candidate timeout marks `TIMEOUT` and campaign continues.
>   - `--resume` skips completed candidates and appends missing rows only.
>   - Candidate selection never reads HSPICE correlation files.
>   - HSPICE decks always use local copied `input_channel.sNp`.
>   - Preprocessing variants preserve port count, Z0, and original evaluation grid.
> - Integration checks:
>
>   - Clarity: expected fast-edge failures remain visible; 500 ps should pass if current behavior holds.
>   - `ntwk2/ntwk3`: slower edges should correlate well; 5 ps should remain WARN unless tuning improves it.
>   - Cisco `.s4p`: full vector-fit candidates must not be falsely marked full-ready if RX/TX/reflection disagree.
>   - Molex `.s4p`: verify selected model, ngspice smoke, HSPICE audit, and share-pack artifacts.
>   - Full run must produce all CSVs, selected models, plots, and package outputs without manual cleanup.
> - Acceptance criteria:
>
>   - No candidate with non-passive dense response, unstable ngspice output, nonfinite waveform, severe pre-response, or failed export can receive `FULL_MODEL_READY`.
>   - Independent `FULL_MODEL_READY` false-pass rate versus HSPICE must be below 5% on holdout cases.
>   - Any false pass must map to a named missing metric before thresholds are promoted.
>   - The final report must clearly say whether scikit-rf vector fitting is production-ready, scoped-ready, or still research-only.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Use scikit-rf `1.12.0` from `$env:TEMP\ibis_skrf_target`.
> - Selectable SPICE models use `parameter_type='s'` and `write_spice_subcircuit_s`.
> - `fit_proportional=True` and non-S-parameter fits are diagnostic-only until export behavior is proven safe.
> - HSPICE remains audit-only and never changes `vf_ranking.csv`.
> - Default production target is full multiport ngspice simulation with 50 ohm digital transient validation first; arbitrary nonlinear/termination claims require stricter future validation.

</details>

The installed API confirms more knobs than we’re currently using: `auto_fit` has initial poles/add/iterations/alpha/gamma/nu_samples, and `passivity_enforce` has samples/fmax/preserve_dc. The current script only sweeps a small subset, so the next campaign should extend the grid and add timeouts/checkpointing before going broad.

I analyzed the overnight run and wrote the summary here: [OVERNIGHT_ANALYSIS.md](./results/sparam_vector_fit_campaign_v2_phase1_overnight_2026-06-18/OVERNIGHT_ANALYSIS.md).

**Bottom Line**
The vector-fit path is showing real promise for some 2-port cases, but it is not ready as a general full-model ngspice S-parameter flow yet.

The good news: `ntwk2` and `ntwk3` correlate very well with HSPICE at 50 ps and 500 ps edges. RX RMSE is roughly sub-mV to about 1.3 mV, which is genuinely encouraging.

The bad news: Clarity still fails fast-edge RX shape at 5 ps and 50 ps. It only passes cleanly at 500 ps. Also, the Cisco `.s4p` full vector-fit path did not produce selected full models, while the reduced RX baseline still looks more useful for Cisco RX voltage shape.

**Key Numbers**

- Candidate metric rows: `5970`
- Ranked channels: `9`
- Selected vector models: `6`
- HSPICE audit rows: `54`
- RX/TX overlay PNGs: `84`
- Share-pack files: `584`

Selected-model HSPICE audit:

- 5 ps edge: `4 WARN`, `2 FAIL`
- 50 ps edge: `4 PASS`, `2 FAIL`
- 500 ps edge: `6 PASS`

So the pattern is very clear: slower edges match much better; fast-edge behavior is still the weak point.

**Important Tooling Issue**
Some HSPICE audit rows are marked `ERROR`, but that was not a physics/model failure. HSPICE ran; ngspice failed to include some generated `.sp` files because the candidate model path was too long, around 266 characters. We should fix the audit runner to copy the vector-fit `.sp` into the local audit folder under a short filename before including it.

> explain in more details, what's current findings and next steps

**Current Finding**
The vector-fit campaign is useful, but it is telling us “not ready as a universal flow yet.”

The cleanest result is this: scikit-rf vector fitting can produce ngspice `.sp` models that correlate very well with HSPICE for some 2-port channels, especially `ntwk2` and `ntwk3`, once the edge is not extremely fast.

For selected models:

| Case             |                      5 ps edge |             50 ps edge |            500 ps edge |
| ---------------- | -----------------------------: | ---------------------: | ---------------------: |
| `ntwk2`        | WARN, RX RMSE about`1.35 mV` | PASS, about`0.36 mV` | PASS, about`0.31 mV` |
| `ntwk3`        | WARN, RX RMSE about`0.99 mV` | PASS, about`0.37 mV` | PASS, about`0.14 mV` |
| Clarity original |         FAIL, about`23.3 mV` | FAIL, about`12.0 mV` |  PASS, about`4.7 mV` |
| Clarity fitted   |         FAIL, about`17.8 mV` | FAIL, about`21.4 mV` |  PASS, about`2.2 mV` |

So yes: slower edges match much better. The 500 ps edge is very encouraging. The 50 ps edge works for `ntwk2/ntwk3` but not Clarity. The 5 ps edge is still the weak point.

**What This Means**
The frequency-domain fit alone is not enough.

Some vector-fit candidates had excellent S-parameter fit, passivity looked okay, and independent metrics called them PASS. But HSPICE still showed WARN/FAIL for fast-edge transient behavior. After fixing the audit path issue, the top-K independent PASS rows correlated as:

- HSPICE PASS: `20`
- HSPICE WARN: `8`
- HSPICE FAIL: `8`
- HSPICE ERROR: `0`

That is too many false clean-PASS cases. So our current independent PASS criteria are still too optimistic.

**Important Detail**
The selected models themselves were conservative: no selected model is currently `FULL_MODEL_READY`. The selected models are WARN/FAIL after ngspice smoke. That is good behavior from the pipeline. The risk appeared in top-K candidates where raw frequency/passivity metrics looked strong but HSPICE exposed fast-edge mismatch.

**Vector Fit vs Reduced Model**
Right now:

- Vector fit is better for pursuing a true full `.sNp -> SPICE` model.
- Reduced models are still better for Cisco RX-through behavior today.
- Reduced Cisco `.s4p` models can match RX voltage shape, but they are scoped models, not full 4-port replacements.
- Full vector-fit `.s4p` failed to produce selected models for the Cisco channels in this run.

So the current practical answer is: reduced model remains our best RX-through demo path; vector fit remains the correct research path for full model trust.

**Preprocessing Finding**
Raw Touchstone data won.

The selected vector-fit models all came from `raw` preprocessing. `dc_hold`, frequency trimming, `hf_hold`, and high-frequency rolloff did not produce selected models in this run. That does not mean those are useless forever, but in this campaign they did not beat raw fitting.

**Passivity Enforcement Finding**
Passivity enforcement helps some cases, but it is not a magic fix.

For `ntwk2`, the selected model was a passivity-enforced `vector_12r12c` candidate. But for Clarity, passivity-enforced candidates still failed HSPICE fast-edge behavior. So passivity is necessary for trust, but not sufficient.

**Next Steps**

1. Tighten independent PASS rules.
   A model should not get clean PASS if 5 ps or 50 ps edge smoke shows RX overshoot, undershoot, ringing ambiguity, or active-window shape mismatch. Fast-edge behavior needs to be a first-class gate.
2. Add a Touchstone-derived time-domain metric.
   We need to compute an independent step/impulse response from the original S-parameter and compare the vector-fit model against that before HSPICE. This is likely the missing predictor for Clarity-style failures.
3. Split readiness labels.
   We should report:

   - `SLOW_EDGE_READY`
   - `RX_SHAPE_READY`
   - `FAST_EDGE_WARN`
   - `FULL_MODEL_READY`

   Right now, saying only PASS/WARN/FAIL hides the useful fact that some models are very good at 50 ps/500 ps but not 5 ps.
4. Push `.s4p` vector fitting separately.
   Cisco full vector-fit failed fit gates. Next we should try delay extraction, differential/common-mode transform, and maybe lower-complexity staged fitting before trying to fit the whole 4-port matrix directly.
5. Use reduced RX as the benchmark, not the enemy.
   For Cisco, reduced RX-through is still our best visible result. Vector fitting should be compared against it channel by channel.

The current evidence is good progress: we now have a working campaign, clean overlays, zero audit errors, and a clear technical weakness to attack next: independent fast-edge transient prediction.

I pushed the vector-fitting workflow in the direction that gives us the clearest high-impact result for tomorrow: an HSPICE-independent fast-edge trust gate.

**What I Added**
I updated [run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py](./scripts/run_sparam_vector_fit_campaign.py) with an edge-bandwidth readiness metric:

```text
required bandwidth = 0.35 / edge_time
```

So:

```text
5 ps   -> ~70 GHz required
50 ps  -> ~7 GHz required
500 ps -> ~0.7 GHz required
```

This is now reported per selected model and used to downgrade future candidate PASS claims when the Touchstone bandwidth is not enough for the edge rate being claimed.

**Why This Matters**
This explains the overnight HSPICE correlation very cleanly:

- 5 ps edges need ~70 GHz. Our audited cases do not have enough bandwidth, and HSPICE showed `0 PASS / 12 WARN / 6 FAIL`.
- 50 ps edges need ~7 GHz. `ntwk2/ntwk3` have 10 GHz data and passed HSPICE; Clarity has only 2 GHz data and failed.
- 500 ps edges need ~0.7 GHz. All audited rows had enough bandwidth and all passed HSPICE.

That gives us a strong, simple story: the vector-fit itself is not the only issue; some edge-rate claims are unsupported by the source S-parameter bandwidth.

**New High-Impact Result**
After applying the edge-bandwidth gate, adjusted independent PASS correlates cleanly on this dataset:

```text
Adjusted independent PASS: HSPICE P/W/F/E = 20/0/0/0
False PASS rate = 0.0
```

That is the strongest progress result so far. Small dataset, yes, but this is exactly the kind of predictor we need.

- [OVERNIGHT_ANALYSIS.md](./results/sparam_vector_fit_campaign_v2_phase1_overnight_2026-06-18/OVERNIGHT_ANALYSIS.md)

```text

vf_edge_bandwidth_calibration.csv
vf_edge_adjusted_calibration_summary.csv
vf_edge_adjusted_hspice_correlation.csv
```

**Next Step**
The next high-value move is to rerun a broader dataset with this gate active, especially more Cisco/repo-local channels. The goal for tomorrow should be:

```text
Show that edge-adjusted independent PASS stays low false-pass across more channels.
```

I found **12 `.sp` files**, but they collapse to **6 unique netlists** because `history\1` and `history\2` are mostly duplicated snapshots.

**Big Picture**
This folder is a Cadence Topology Workbench / Sigrity SPDSIM export for the Cadence example IBIS model:

```text
scd_example.ibs
component: ABC_Serdes
Tx model: sla_out
Rx model: sla_in
data rate: 10 Gbps
```

Important: these decks are **not self-contained**. They reference absolute paths from the machine/project that generated them, for example:

```text
C:\Cadence\SPB_25.1\share\topxp\SerialLink\ibis_sparam_thru\scd_example.ibs
C:\Users\simonhwang_pcbauto\my_top\result\S1.sp
C:\Cadence\SPB_25.1\share\topxp\standard_step.sp
```

Those paths do **not** exist on this machine as-is, so the decks would need path repair and Cadence/SPDSIM support to rerun directly.

**Files Found**

```text
result\Tx_scd_example.sp
result\Rx_scd_example.sp

history\1\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
history\1\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_ibis.sp
history\1\sparam\1\SParamExtraction.sp

history\2\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
history\2\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_ibis.sp
history\2\sparam\1\SParamExtraction.sp

history\buffer\1\simulation_input.sp
history\buffer\1\simulation_ibis_definition.sp
history\buffer\2\simulation_input.sp
history\buffer\2\simulation_ibis_definition.sp
```

`history\1` and `history\2` versions are byte-identical for the `.sp` files.

**What Each Group Is**

`result\Tx_scd_example.sp`
This defines extracted Tx-side component wrapper fragments for `Tx_ABC_Serdes`. It contains:

```text
.subckt Tx_ABC_Serdes 6 7 1 10 in
.subckt Tx_ABC_Serdes_OnDie_RC
.subckt Tx_ABC_Serdes_Pin_RLC
.subckt onpkg_RLC
.subckt Tx_ABC_Serdes_PkgModel
```

It maps pins `6/7` to `out1p/out1n`, power `1` to `vdd`, ground `10` to `vss`, and includes generated package/on-die parasitic templates. The package values are tiny:

```text
R_pkg = 2e-3
L_pkg = 2e-10
C_pkg = 2e-13
```

But the top-level `Tx_ABC_Serdes` body is mostly metadata; the active IBIS behavior is in the history-generated IBIS definition files.

`result\Rx_scd_example.sp`
Same idea for Rx. It defines:

```text
.subckt Rx_ABC_Serdes 8 9 1 10 rxnode
.subckt Rx_ABC_Serdes_OnDie_RC
.subckt Rx_ABC_Serdes_Pin_RLC
.subckt onpkg_RLC
.subckt Rx_ABC_Serdes_PkgModel
```

Pins `8/9` are `in1p/in1n`, and `rxnode` is the observed differential receive output. Again, this is mostly wrapper/parasitic structure.

`history\...\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp`
This is the **main transient channel deck**. It connects:

```text
Tx IBIS buffer -> 4-port S-parameter block -> Rx IBIS buffer
```

Topology:

```text
X1 n1 n2 pwr1 gnd in     Tx_ABC_Serdes
X2 n1 gnd n2 n3 gnd n4   S1_sparams_4port_bnp
X3 n3 n4 pwr2 gnd rxnode Rx_ABC_Serdes
Xstim in gnd standard_step
.tran 2p 30n
```

It prints:

```text
V(in)
V(rxnode)
V(n3)
V(n4)
```

So this is the deck most analogous to the Tx/channel/Rx transient tests we have been doing.

`history\...\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_ibis.sp`
This defines the behavioral Tx and Rx subcircuits used by the main channel deck. It uses Cadence/SPDSIM IBIS `B_...` elements like:

```text
B_SpeedXP_auto_6 ... file='...\scd_example.ibs' model='sla_out' buffer=output
B_SpeedXP_auto_8 ... file='...\scd_example.ibs' model='sla_in'  buffer=input
```

The Tx side generates the complementary input internally:

```text
einn inn 10 volt='1-v(in, 10)'
```

The Rx side creates:

```text
erxnode rxnode 10 volt='v(8, 9)'
```

So `rxnode` is simply the differential voltage between Rx pins 8 and 9.

`history\...\SParamExtraction.sp`
This is a small **S-parameter extraction deck**. It instantiates the 4-port channel and attaches 50 ohm SPDSIM ports:

```text
Port_1 n1 gnd port=1 z0=50 ac=1
Port_2 n2 gnd port=2 z0=50
Port_3 n3 gnd port=3 z0=50
Port_4 n4 gnd port=4 z0=50
.ac lin 10 0 1e+09
.lin filename=S_para format=bnp
```

It outputs a Cadence binary `.bnp` S-parameter file, not Touchstone. There is a local `S_para_S_diff.bnp`, but the deck itself includes missing `S1.sp`.

`history\buffer\...\simulation_input.sp`
This is a short **Tx buffer-only transient deck**. It instantiates the Tx model and a test fixture:

```text
X1 n1 n2 n3 gnd Tx_ABC_Serdes
X2 n1 n2 n3 gnd Tx_ABC_Serdes_Test_Fixture
.tran 2p 2n
.print V(n1) V(n2) V(n1,n2)
```

But it includes an absolute path to `simulation_ibis_definition.sp` from the original creator’s machine, so the include path is stale.

`history\buffer\...\simulation_ibis_definition.sp`
This is the buffer-only IBIS definition. It defines explicit complementary PWL input sources:

```text
stimulusout1p: 0 -> 1 -> 0
stimulusout1n: 1 -> 0 -> 1
```

and uses the same `sla_out` output buffer from `scd_example.ibs`. The fixture terminates each output through `50 ohm` to `0.9 V`.

**Important Finding**
SPDSIM already warned about bandwidth:

```text
Warning 5000: The bandwidth of the 'X2.S' S-parameter is insufficient ...
Set the time step to 10.0 ps and rerun the simulation.
```

The buffer delay file says the differential output transition is about `5.68 ps` typ. So this example has the same theme we just found in the vector-fit work: the driver edge is very fast, while the available S-parameter bandwidth may not support that edge rate cleanly.

**Conclusion**
These are Cadence-generated SPDSIM decks for an IBIS Tx/Rx + 4-port channel example. The most relevant files for us are:

```text
channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_ibis.sp
SParamExtraction.sp
```

But they are not directly portable to ngspice/HSPICE yet because they rely on Cadence IBIS `B_` elements, `.bnp` S-parameter handling, `standard_step.sp`, and missing absolute-path includes.

> so the syntax is pretty much hspice sompatible?

Yes, for `simulation_input.sp`, the syntax is pretty much HSPICE-compatible.

The important evidence is that HSPICE accepted these Cadence-generated IBIS buffer elements:

```spice
B_SpeedXP_auto_6 ...
+ file = '...\scd_example.ibs'
+ model = 'sla_out'
+ buffer = output
```

and completed the transient simulation with a valid `.tr0`.

What was not portable was mainly the **paths**, not the syntax:

```spice
.inc 'C:\Users\simonhwang_pcbauto\...'
file = 'C:\Cadence\SPB_25.1\...scd_example.ibs'
```

After patching those to local files / installed Cadence 24.1 paths, HSPICE ran.

Caveat: this was the **buffer-only deck**. The main channel deck also uses a Cadence-generated 4-port S-parameter subckt:

```spice
X2 ... S1_sparams_4port_bnp
```

That may need more work because it depends on `S1.sp` / `.bnp` channel model handling. But the IBIS `B_` buffer syntax itself is HSPICE-compatible enough for this case.

> ngspice has B-element?

Yes, ngspice has a `B` source, but **not the same kind** as HSPICE/Cadence IBIS `B` element.

In ngspice, `B` is a behavioral source, for example:

```spice
B1 out 0 V = {sin(2*pi*1e6*time)}
B2 out 0 I = {V(in)/50}
```

It supports equations/expressions for voltage or current.

But the Cadence/HSPICE deck uses `B` like this:

```spice
B_SpeedXP_auto_6 pwr gnd out in pwr gnd
+ file = 'scd_example.ibs'
+ model = 'sla_out'
+ buffer = output
+ ramp_fwf = 0
+ ramp_rwf = 0
```

That is an **IBIS buffer element**, not a plain behavioral equation source. HSPICE understands that as an IBIS model instance. ngspice will not understand `file=... model=... buffer=output` on a `B` element.

So:

```text
ngspice B-element: yes, behavioral source
HSPICE/Cadence B-element here: IBIS buffer instance
Compatible directly: no
```

For ngspice, we would need to translate the IBIS buffer into something ngspice can run, for example:

- pybis-generated behavioral subcircuit,
- our existing ngspice+pybis flow,
- a reduced/linearized driver model,
- or a custom B-source approximation derived from the IBIS V/T and I/V tables.

> so both SPICE have B-element, just different meaning

Exactly.

Both use the letter `B`, but they mean different things.

In **ngspice**:

```spice
B1 out 0 V = {expression}
B2 out 0 I = {expression}
```

`B` means a behavioral voltage/current source defined by equations.

In **HSPICE / Cadence-generated IBIS decks**:

```spice
B_drv pwr gnd out in pwr gnd
+ file = 'model.ibs'
+ model = 'sla_out'
+ buffer = output
```

`B` can mean an IBIS buffer instance that loads an `.ibs` file and evaluates the IBIS model.

So the name is the same, but the parser semantics are not.

That is why the generated deck is HSPICE-compatible after path fixes, but not directly ngspice-compatible. Ngspice would need a translated IBIS model, not this HSPICE-style `B ... file=... model=... buffer=...` syntax.

> how about behavior sources in hspice ,what does it called?

In HSPICE, behavioral sources are usually called **dependent sources with behavioral expressions**, often using:

```spice
E
G
```

or HSPICE’s behavioral form:

```spice
Ename n+ n- VOL='expression'
Gname n+ n- CUR='expression'
```

Examples:

```spice
Ebuf out 0 VOL='2*V(in)'
Gload out 0 CUR='V(out)/50'
```

There are also standard dependent-source forms:

```spice
E1 out 0 in 0 10      * voltage-controlled voltage source
G1 out 0 in 0 0.02    * voltage-controlled current source
```

So roughly:

```text
ngspice behavioral source: B
HSPICE behavioral voltage source: E ... VOL='...'
HSPICE behavioral current source: G ... CUR='...'
```

And separately, in HSPICE IBIS flow, `B` is used for **IBIS buffer instances**, like:

```spice
Bdrv ...
+ file='model.ibs'
+ model='...'
+ buffer=output
```

That is why `B` is overloaded across simulators.

> check my understnading: simulation_input.sp is the testbench that drive the Tx buffer into a pure 50 ohm load with PWL sources, so it's a chacterization testbench, not the actual simluation testbench that contains channel info

Yes, that understanding is correct.

`simulation_input.sp` is a **Tx buffer characterization testbench**, not the actual channel simulation.

It does this:

```spice
X1 n1 n2 n3 gnd Tx_ABC_Serdes
X2 n1 n2 n3 gnd Tx_ABC_Serdes_Test_Fixture
```

Where:

- `X1` is the Tx IBIS buffer.
- `X2` is a simple fixture.
- The fixture provides complementary PWL stimulus internally and terminates the outputs through `50 ohm` loads to `0.9 V`.

Inside `simulation_ibis_definition.sp`:

```spice
r_6 in_6 out_6 50
v_6 out_6 in_10 0.9

r_7 in_7 out_7 50
v_7 out_7 in_10 0.9
```

So the Tx outputs see simple 50 ohm pullups/load references, not a channel.

The **actual channel simulation testbench** is:

```text
history\1\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
```

or the duplicate:

```text
history\2\1\Chan_Typ_Typ\channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
```

That one connects:

```spice
Tx buffer -> S1_sparams_4port_bnp channel -> Rx buffer
```

So yes: `simulation_input.sp` is for buffer behavior/edge characterization; `channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp` is the actual Tx-channel-Rx transient simulation.

> ok back to vector fitting

Back to vector fitting. Current best result:

We added the **edge-bandwidth readiness gate**, and it gave us the cleanest progress so far:

```text
required bandwidth = 0.35 / edge_time
```

On the audited vector-fit dataset:

```text
Edge-adjusted independent PASS:
HSPICE P/W/F/E = 20/0/0/0
false-pass rate = 0.0
```

That means the new independent gate removed the false clean-PASS cases we saw before. The story is now much stronger:

- Clarity has only `2 GHz` S-parameter bandwidth.
  - 5 ps needs ~`70 GHz` -> not trustworthy.
  - 50 ps needs ~`7 GHz` -> not enough.
  - 500 ps needs ~`0.7 GHz` -> okay, and HSPICE passed.
- `ntwk2/ntwk3` have `10 GHz` bandwidth.
  - 50 ps and 500 ps passed.
  - 5 ps still not enough.

The immediate next move should be to broaden this result:

1. Run a larger vector-fit audit with the new edge-bandwidth gate active.
2. Include more repo-local and Cisco channels.
3. Report whether adjusted independent PASS still predicts HSPICE PASS.
4. Keep selected models scoped by edge readiness, not just generic PASS/WARN/FAIL.

The main artifacts to show tomorrow are:

```text
results/sparam_vector_fit_campaign_v2_phase1_overnight_2026-06-18/README.md
```

> ok so explain the real flow, i assume simulation_input.sp is run first, then its result is used in chanel_Tx_out.....sp?

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I’ll pin this to the actual files so the flow is clear, because there are two “characterization” ideas mixed together here: buffer delay characterization and channel impulse characterization.

</details>

Not exactly. `simulation_input.sp` is a separate Tx buffer delay/characterization run, not the direct input waveform file for `channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp`.

The real flow looks like this:

```text
TopXP project/settings
        |
        |-- optional Tx buffer delay characterization
        |      history/buffer/1/simulation_input.sp
        |      Tx IBIS -> 50 ohm loads
        |      measures Tx buffer timing/delay metadata
        |
        |-- channel model / S-parameter block
        |      S1 = sparams_4port.bnp via S1.sp wrapper
        |
        |-- channel transient characterization
        |      channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
        |      Tx IBIS -> S-parameter channel -> Rx IBIS
        |      driven by standard_step
        |      produces channel Tx/Rx characterization waveforms
        |
        |-- AMI/statistical eye flow
               command.txt / spdut.log
               consumes channel_Tx..._tx.cur and channel_Tx..._rx.cur
               applies random data + Tx/Rx AMI models
```

So `simulation_input.sp` may be run earlier by TopXP to measure Tx buffer delay. We see that reflected in `channel_result.xml`, where the Tx signal settings contain values like:

```text
riseBufferDelay = 1.3626e-11
fallBufferDelay = 2.15e-12
```

But `channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp` does not include or read the `.tr0` result from `simulation_input.sp`.

The actual channel deck is the important one for channel characterization:

```spice
X1 n1 n2 pwr1 gnd in
+ Tx_ABC_Serdes

X2 n1 gnd n2 n3 gnd n4
+ S1_sparams_4port_bnp

X3 n3 n4 pwr2 gnd rxnode
+ Rx_ABC_Serdes

Xstim in gnd standard_step tdel = 0n
.tran 2p 30n
```

That means:

```text
standard_step -> Tx IBIS buffer -> 4-port S-parameter channel -> Rx IBIS input
```

Then the later TopXP/AMI flow uses the channel characterization files. In `command.txt`, the AMI flow references:

```text
channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_tx.cur
channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_rx.cur
```

So the clean correction is:

`simulation_input.sp` is a preliminary buffer-only characterization deck.
`channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp` is the real channel transient characterization deck.
The `.cur` output from the channel deck, not `simulation_input.sp`, is what feeds the later AMI/statistical eye flow.

> ok so the actual simlation deck need: the channel sp wrapper, the ibis sp wrapper, and implicitly the results from simulation_input.sp?

Almost, but I’d phrase it slightly differently:

The actual channel simulation deck needs:

1. The channel SP wrapper: `S1.sp`, wrapping `sparams_4port.bnp`
2. The IBIS SP wrapper: `channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx_ibis.sp`
3. The stimulus include: `standard_step.sp`
4. The underlying IBIS file: `scd_example.ibs`

It does not directly need the raw results from `simulation_input.sp`.

What is “implicit” is only the buffer delay metadata. TopXP appears to have used the buffer characterization flow to compute Tx rise/fall delay values, and those values are recorded in `channel_result.xml`:

```text
riseBufferDelay = 13.626 ps
fallBufferDelay = 2.15 ps
```

But the HSPICE deck we ran does not read a `.tr0`, `.csv`, or waveform generated by `simulation_input.sp`.

So:

```text
simulation_input.sp
    -> buffer delay characterization metadata
    -> may inform TopXP's higher-level channel/AMI setup

channel_Tx_out1p_out1n_Rx.sp
    -> real channel transient deck
    -> runs from IBIS + S-parameter channel + standard_step
    -> produces channel characterization waveforms
```

For reproducing the HSPICE transient deck itself, the required files are the wrappers and model files, not the previous `simulation_input.sp` result.

Key result: the agreement is very good for this fixture.

- Pad waveform active-window RMSE: `5.26 mV`
- Pad waveform max abs error: `16.78 mV`
- Ku active-window RMSE: `0.00436`
- Kd active-window RMSE: `0.00536`

The HSPICE and ngspice decks are also copied into the result folder, along with raw/tr0/log outputs and [metrics_summary.csv](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_overlay_2026-06-18/metrics_summary.csv). The caveat is that this follows the switching-coefficient extraction style: 0/3.3 V PWL input, 1 ps edges, 50 ohm + 2 pF load.

> so the switching coefficient turns out to be aligning very well, for ngspice vs. hspice?

Yes. For this `io_buf.ibs` switching-coefficient fixture, pybis+ngspice and HSPICE native IBIS align very well.

The coefficient comparison is especially strong:

- `Ku` active-window RMSE: `0.00436`
- `Kd` active-window RMSE: `0.00536`
- max coefficient error: about `0.023`

And the pad waveform also lines up closely:

- pad voltage RMSE: `5.26 mV`
- pad voltage max error: `16.78 mV`

So the main takeaway is: the IBIS switching functions themselves are not the big mismatch source here. For this clean 50 ohm + 2 pF coefficient-extraction bench, pybis reproduces the HSPICE native IBIS Ku/Kd behavior very closely.

The remaining mismatches we saw elsewhere are more likely coming from bench/channel interaction, edge-rate assumptions, package/channel modeling, or simulator/model implementation details around the larger setup, rather than pybis generating totally different switching coefficients.

[metrics_by_case.csv](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/metrics_by_case.csv)
[summary plot](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/plots/summary_rmse_by_case.png)
[case plots folder](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/plots/cases)

**What I changed**
The HSPICE and ngspice benches are generated consistently per case, changing:

- input edge rate: `1 ps`, `5 ps`, `50 ps`, `500 ps`, `2 ns`
- load: `50 ohm only`, `50 ohm + 2 pF`, `50 ohm + 10 pF`, `25 ohm + 2 pF`, `100 ohm + 2 pF`
- stimulus pattern: normal rise/fall, double toggle, short 2 ns pulse
- one exploratory threshold case: `1.8 V` input high

**Headline result**
The switching coefficients align very well for normal sharp/full switching and load variation:

- `GOOD`: 7 cases
- `WARN`: 2 cases
- `CHECK`: 3 cases
- `FAIL`: 0 cases

The weak point is not load. The weak point is input-stimulus/state-machine behavior:

- 1 ps baseline: `GOOD`, pad RMSE `5.289 mV`
- double toggle: `GOOD`, pad RMSE `5.713 mV`
- load sweeps: all `GOOD`
- 5 ps / 50 ps edges: `WARN`
- 500 ps / 2 ns edges: `CHECK`
- short 2 ns pulse: `CHECK`, largest mismatch

So the refined conclusion is: pybis/ngspice matches HSPICE native IBIS Ku/Kd very well for fast, complete digital toggles, even across load changes. But slow analog input ramps and interrupted transitions expose real differences in how the two flows handle IBIS switching state.

> analyze clear these latest result. what kind of setup have big mismatch?

The latest sweep says the big mismatch is **not mainly from output load**. It is mainly from **input switching/state-machine behavior**.

**Big Mismatch Setups**
The largest mismatches happen when the input stimulus is not a clean, fast, complete digital transition:

| Case                     |                                                 What changed |   Pad RMSE |      Ku/Kd RMSE | Result         |
| ------------------------ | -----------------------------------------------------------: | ---------: | --------------: | -------------- |
| `edge_2ns_50r_2pf`     |                                    very slow 2 ns input edge | `393 mV` | `0.28 / 0.34` | big mismatch   |
| `short_pulse_2ns_high` | output begins switching, then input reverses before settling | `361 mV` | `0.28 / 0.23` | big mismatch   |
| `edge_500ps_50r_2pf`   |                                       slow 500 ps input edge | `135 mV` | `0.10 / 0.13` | clear mismatch |

These cases show HSPICE native IBIS and pybis/ngspice choosing different Ku/Kd trajectories. In other words, the mismatch is around **how the IBIS switching coefficients evolve when the input transition is slow or interrupted**.

**Moderate Mismatch**
These are not terrible, but no longer “excellent”:

| Case                  |     Pad RMSE |        Ku/Kd RMSE | Result  |
| --------------------- | -----------: | ----------------: | ------- |
| `edge_5ps_50r_2pf`  |  `7.93 mV` | `0.015 / 0.021` | warning |
| `edge_50ps_50r_2pf` | `11.37 mV` | `0.010 / 0.015` | warning |

Even at 5 ps and 50 ps, coefficient mismatch grows compared with the 1 ps baseline. The pad waveform is still pretty close, but the switching coefficients already start drifting.

**Good Setups**
These match well:

| Case type                      | Finding                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| 1 ps normal rise/fall          | very good match                        |
| double toggle with 1 ps edges  | very good match                        |
| 25 ohm / 50 ohm / 100 ohm load | still good                             |
| 0 pF / 2 pF / 10 pF load       | still good                             |
| 1.8 V high exploratory case    | surprisingly still close in this bench |

So for **fast, complete digital toggles**, pybis/ngspice tracks HSPICE native IBIS well. Changing the load does not break the match.

**Main Conclusion**
The big mismatch setups are:

1. **Slow input ramps**: `500 ps`, especially `2 ns`.
2. **Interrupted switching**: short pulse where the input reverses before the output finishes transitioning.
3. Probably any setup where the input behaves more like an analog ramp than a clean digital decision.

That points to the key difference: HSPICE’s native IBIS implementation has its own switching-state logic, while pybis expands the model into explicit free-SPICE behavioral sources. They agree when the input decisively changes state, but diverge when the input transition gives the state machine ambiguity.

I dug into the mismatch cases and wrote the detailed analysis here:

[SWITCHING_COEFF_MISMATCH_ANALYSIS.md](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/mismatch_analysis/SWITCHING_COEFF_MISMATCH_ANALYSIS.md)

Key data files:

[mismatch_case_summary.csv](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/mismatch_analysis/mismatch_case_summary.csv)
[mismatch_event_timing.csv](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/mismatch_analysis/mismatch_event_timing.csv)
[diagnostic plots](./results/io_buf_switching_coeff_sweep_2026-06-19/mismatch_analysis/plots)

**Main finding:** there are two different mismatch mechanisms.

**1. Slow-edge cases are mostly coefficient timing skew**

For `500 ps` and `2 ns` input ramps, HSPICE and pybis both eventually use roughly the same coefficient states, but they start/stop the transitions at different times.

- `edge_500ps`: pybis is about `+100 ps` later than HSPICE on the rising transition, then about `-175 ps` earlier on the falling transition.
- `edge_2ns`: pybis is about `+370 ps` later on rise, then about `-720 ps` earlier on fall.

So relative to pybis, HSPICE effectively makes the output high interval wider for very slow ramps: it turns on earlier and turns off later. That directly creates the large pad mismatch.

**2. Short-pulse case is a state/amplitude mismatch, not just timing**

For `short_pulse_2ns_high`, the output transition gets interrupted before the pad settles.

Here HSPICE behaves more conservatively:

- HSPICE Ku only partially turns on, peaking around mid-level.
- pybis Ku jumps close to full `1.0`.
- Result: ngspice/pybis produces a much larger pad pulse than HSPICE.

That is why the short-pulse case is so bad: pybis treats the pull-up state as much more fully active, while HSPICE keeps the switching coefficient history-limited/partial.

**What this means**

For normal fast digital toggles, Ku/Kd alignment is very good. The mismatch appears when the input stimulus creates ambiguous switching state:

- slow analog-like input ramps
- interrupted transitions
- cases where the input reverses before the IBIS output waveform has finished

So the next thing to verify is likely HSPICE’s exact trigger/state logic for `Vinl/Vinh` and waveform interpolation during slow or interrupted input transitions. That is where pybis and native HSPICE are behaving differently.

[make_io_buf_interrupted_switching_demo.py](./scripts/make_io_buf_interrupted_switching_demo.py)

The demo’s main story is:

- Normal settled high from the full-toggle case is about `1.545 V`.
- In the interrupted case, the reverse command arrives when the pad is only `0.266 V`, so the first transition clearly has not settled.
- HSPICE keeps the pull-up coefficient partial: Ku peaks at only `0.543`.
- pybis lets Ku go nearly full-on: Ku peaks at `1.013`.
- That creates a much larger pad pulse:
  - HSPICE pad peak: `0.825 V`
  - pybis pad peak: `1.521 V`
- Kd recovery in pybis is also about `360 ps` later than HSPICE.

So the demo shows visually that this is not just a small timing offset. It is a coefficient-history/state behavior difference when a new switching command interrupts the previous output transition.

Yes, correct. We already have BBS automation in two places:

1. Standalone BBS wrapper:
   [bbs_extract.py](./scripts/bbs_extract.py)

This directly calls Cadence Sigrity `BroadbandSPICE.exe`, generates a temporary Sigrity Python script, loads the `.sNp`, sets BBS options, and exports a SPICE circuit.

2. Integrated study workflow:
   [run_sparam_conversion_quality_study.py](./scripts/run_sparam_conversion_quality_study.py)

This has `--enable-bbs`, which makes BBS a first-class candidate family alongside our reduced/vector-fit models. It can generate both:

- `hspice` compatible BBS model
- `gspice` / General SPICE compatible BBS model for ngspice

Typical command shape:

```powershell
py -3.14 scripts\run_sparam_conversion_quality_study.py qualify `
  --study-dir results\bbs_test `
  --extra-touchstone-dir hspice\sparam `
  --enable-bbs `
  --bbs-modes passivity2 `
  --bbs-circuit-types hspice,gspice `
  --bbs-preset-grid clean `
  --bbs-timeout 600
```

It expects BroadbandSPICE here by default:

```text
C:\Cadence\Sigrity2024.1\tools\bin\BroadbandSPICE.exe
```

or you can override with:

```powershell
--bbs-exe "C:\path\to\BroadbandSPICE.exe"
```

Outputs include:

- `bbs_candidates.csv`
- `bbs_metrics.csv`
- `bbs_ranking.csv`
- `bbs_ngspice_smoke.csv`
- `bbs_hspice_correlation.csv`
- `selected_models/bbs/`
- `plots/bbs_overlays/`
- `bbs_audit_share_pack/`

So yes: we already have an automatic script path to call Broadband SPICE and convert `.sNp -> SPICE`, plus ngspice/HSPICE validation hooks.

What I verified:

- All copied `Clarity_example.S2P` sources match the same SHA-256 hash, so this is not a stale/wrong file issue.
- The parser is using normal Touchstone 2-port order: `S11, S21, S12, S22`.
- In the original file, `S21` and `S12` are identical and very smooth in dB:
  - `S21/S12 = -0.020 dB` at `50 MHz`
  - `S21/S12 = -0.480 dB` at `2 GHz`
- The orange BBS fitted response has ripple, so visually it makes the original blue curve look suspiciously straight.

> why the result show that the rx side figure decay? is it becasue the input stimulus is just one pulse?

Yes, mostly. The RX waveform decays because this setup is exciting the channel with a single pulse edge, and the Agilent `p1 -> p3` path behaves more like a band-pass/coupled RF path than a DC/baseband digital through channel.

What is happening:

- The input pulse edge has broadband frequency content.
- The Agilent S4P path from `p1` to `p3` passes only some frequency bands and has little/no meaningful DC or low-frequency through behavior.
- So the RX node does not settle to a DC high level. Instead, each edge excites the channel’s impulse response.
- That impulse response rings, then decays back toward 0 V because the port is terminated to 75 ohms and there is no sustained low-frequency/DC transmission to hold a level.

So the decay is expected for this kind of channel/path. It is not just a simulator artifact.

A normal digital interconnect channel would usually have strong low-frequency/DC transmission on the main through path. For that kind of channel, a step/pulse would settle to a new voltage level at RX. Here the Agilent example is useful as a “realistic measured multiport with resonances,” but it is probably not a realistic baseband digital channel for `io_buf`.

Also, because we used only one rise and one fall, you see isolated ring-down events. With a repeated bitstream or PRBS, those ring-downs would overlap from edge to edge.

> now abour the short pulse handling of pybis, explain why we cannot simply make it so that when a new egde happen before previous one settled, we just point for example, a falling edge before rise settled, why we cannot just ask ku to start at a mid value instead of playing from 1.0 (or the starting point)

<details><summary>3 previous messages</summary>

> I’ll tie this to the actual pybis structure we’ve been using, because the answer depends on what `ku/kd` mean electrically in the generated subcircuit.
>
> That search was too broad, so I’m narrowing it to the converter and one generated pybis subcircuit.
>
> I found the exact generated coefficient logic: `Ku/Kd` are computed from elapsed time since the detected edge, then used to scale pullup/pulldown I/V tables. That confirms why “start from mid-value” is tempting but incomplete.

</details>

Yes, I see the intuition: if a falling edge arrives while the rising edge is only half done, why not start `Ku/Kd` from the current “halfway” state instead of restarting the falling template from its normal initial value?

The short answer: **we probably can improve pybis in that direction, but we cannot do it by only saying “start `Ku` at a mid value.”** `Ku/Kd` are not a complete physical state.

In our generated pybis model, output current is basically:

```spice
Iout = Ku(t) * I_pullup(Vout) + Kd(t) * I_pulldown(Vout) + clamps + C_comp
```

So `Ku` and `Kd` scale the pullup/pulldown I/V tables. The generated subcircuit has elapsed-time tables for rising and falling events, then selects the proper pair:

```spice
B20 KUR0 ... rising Ku waveform
B21 KDR0 ... rising Kd waveform
B22 KUF0 ... falling Ku waveform
B23 KDF0 ... falling Kd waveform
B28 Ku ... selected Ku
B29 Kd ... selected Kd
```

The problem is that those rising/falling `K` waveforms were extracted from **complete clean transitions**: low-to-high starting from a settled low state, or high-to-low starting from a settled high state. A short pulse creates a different situation: the output node, channel, pullup/pulldown strengths, and internal switching state are all somewhere in between.

Why “start from mid `Ku`” is not enough:

1. **`Ku` alone is not the state.**
   You also need `Kd`, output voltage, current load condition, and probably the transition direction/history. A falling edge from `Ku=0.5` could mean many different physical situations.
2. **The falling waveform is not just the rising waveform played backward.**
   IBIS has separate rising/falling V/T data, and the extracted `Ku/Kd` curves can overshoot, go negative, or exceed 1. They are fitting coefficients, not clean 0-to-1 logic progress variables.
3. **The output voltage may not match the coefficient state.**
   With a channel attached, `Vout` may still be ringing or delayed. The driver’s `Ku/Kd` may say “half switched,” but the channel port voltage may be elsewhere. Starting a new table from a guessed `Ku` can create a current discontinuity.
4. **There is no unique inverse mapping.**
   If the output is at 1.2 V, there is not one obvious pair of `Ku/Kd` that caused it. Many coefficient pairs can produce similar voltage depending on load and history.
5. **HSPICE likely uses a proprietary history-aware IBIS event algorithm.**
   Our observation is that HSPICE’s switching coefficients stay much more continuous in interrupted-transition cases. pybis currently behaves more like “detect edge, restart selected waveform template,” which is why short pulses diverge.

The better fix is a **state-continuous retrigger algorithm**, not a simple midpoint reset.

At a new edge, pybis should sample the current state:

```text
current Ku
current Kd
current dKu/dt, dKd/dt maybe
current Vout
new edge direction
```

Then it should choose a new rising/falling trajectory that starts continuously from the current `(Ku,Kd)` pair and moves toward the new final state. A practical version would be:

```text
1. On edge reversal, freeze current Ku/Kd.
2. Find the closest point on the target falling/rising K-curve.
3. Start the new curve from that equivalent time offset.
4. If no good match exists, blend/warp the curve so Ku/Kd are continuous.
5. Limit derivative jumps.
6. Validate against HSPICE switching coefficient traces.
```

So your idea is directionally right: **pybis should not blindly restart from the full-transition starting point when an edge interrupts a previous edge.** But the robust implementation has to preserve both `Ku` and `Kd` continuity and be validated across pulse width/load/edge-rate cases. Otherwise we might make the plotted coefficients look smoother while making the actual output current less physical.

> Plan
>
> # State-Continuous pybis Retrigger Plan
>
> ## Summary
>
> Build an opt-in pybis2spice input-driven model that handles interrupted transitions with continuous internal state instead of restarting every new edge from the beginning of a full IBIS waveform. Validate it against HSPICE native IBIS using the existing `io_buf` switching-coefficient sweep, with special focus on the short-pulse case where pybis currently overdrives `Ku`.
>
> Current baseline to preserve:
>
> - Normal sharp complete edges already match HSPICE well.
> - Load variation is not the weak point.
> - Slow edges and short pulses expose switching-state mismatch.
> - The worst known case is `short_pulse_2ns_high`: HSPICE keeps `Ku` partial, pybis lets `Ku` approach full-on.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Add a new pybis2spice subcircuit mode:
>
>   - Name: `InputDrivenStateContinuous`.
>   - Existing `InputDriven` remains unchanged and stays the default.
>   - Same external pins: `OUT IN EN VCC VSS`.
>   - Exposed diagnostic nodes: `Ku`, `Kd`, plus internal `PSTATE`, `KUTARGET`, `KDTARGET`.
> - Implement the v1 retrigger algorithm in `tools/pybis2spice/pybis2spice/subcircuit.py`:
>
>   - Replace pure elapsed-time restart logic with a continuous transition-progress state `PSTATE`.
>   - `PSTATE=0` means settled low; `PSTATE=1` means settled high.
>   - On rising command, `PSTATE` ramps toward `1` using the IBIS rising waveform duration.
>   - On falling command, `PSTATE` ramps toward `0` using the IBIS falling waveform duration.
>   - Rising table argument: `PSTATE * rising_duration_ns`.
>   - Falling table argument: `(1 - PSTATE) * falling_duration_ns`.
>   - Final `Ku/Kd` are dynamic state variables that follow `KUTARGET/KDTARGET` with a small global smoothing time constant, default `coeff_tau=1p`, to avoid coefficient jumps at retrigger.
>   - Initial condition defaults to settled low: `Ku=0`, `Kd=1`, `PSTATE=0`.
> - Add CLI support:
>
>   - `scripts/convert_ibis_to_pybis.py --subcircuit-type InputDrivenStateContinuous`.
>   - Keep current calls using `InputDriven` unchanged.
>   - Add unit tests for alias normalization and generated netlist structure.
> - Extend the switching-coefficient sweep:
>
>   - Run three flows per case:
>     - HSPICE native IBIS reference.
>     - ngspice legacy pybis `InputDriven`.
>     - ngspice state-continuous pybis `InputDrivenStateContinuous`.

> Explain clearly what was implemented and what's the result?

I implemented an **experimental pybis retrigger mode** called `InputDrivenStateContinuous`.

The old pybis `InputDriven` mode works like this: every new input edge starts a fresh rising or falling `Ku/Kd` waveform based on elapsed time from that edge. That is fine for complete transitions, but it can be wrong for short pulses where a falling edge arrives before the previous rising output transition settles.

The new mode instead adds a continuous internal state:

- `PSTATE = 0`: output state is low
- `PSTATE = 1`: output state is high
- On a rising input command, `PSTATE` ramps toward `1`
- On a falling input command, `PSTATE` ramps back toward `0`
- `Ku/Kd` are generated from that continuous state instead of blindly restarting from a clean full-transition endpoint
- It also exposes diagnostic nodes: `PSTATE`, `KUTARGET`, `KDTARGET`

Files changed:

- [subcircuit.py](./tools/pybis2spice/pybis2spice/subcircuit.py)
- [test_pybis2spice.py](./tools/pybis2spice/test/test_pybis2spice.py)
- [run_io_buf_state_continuous_retrigger.py](./scripts/run_io_buf_state_continuous_retrigger.py)

I then ran a 13-case validation comparing:

1. HSPICE native IBIS
2. ngspice legacy pybis
3. ngspice state-continuous pybis

Results:
[README](./results/io_buf_state_continuous_retrigger_2026-06-20/README.md)

**Main result:** the idea is promising, but not ready as default.

Good:

- `13 / 13` cases completed.
- Most normal single-edge/load cases stayed `GOOD`.
- Short-pulse improvement was large for very short pulses:
  - `short_pulse_1ns_high`: `653 mV` RMSE → `26.7 mV`
  - `short_pulse_500ps_high`: `679 mV` RMSE → `19.7 mV`
- This strongly supports the hypothesis that pybis needs switching-history awareness.

Bad:

- `double_toggle_1ps` regressed badly:
  - legacy: `5.7 mV` RMSE
  - state-continuous: `475.7 mV` RMSE
- `short_pulse_2ns_high` only improved `25%`, not enough.

Conclusion: **state-continuous retrigger is the right direction, but v1 is too aggressive.** Next version should use legacy behavior for mostly-settled normal toggles and only apply state-continuous retrigger logic when a transition is genuinely interrupted.

You’re right. I looked at it again, and the current algorithm is wrong.

The apparent “improvement” is a false pass: for the 1 ns short pulse, the state-continuous model makes the pad waveform small, but only because it mostly suppresses the driver. It keeps `Kd` near `1` and `Ku` near `0`, while HSPICE actually turns `Kd` off and produces a small partial pulse. So the pad RMSE looked better for the wrong physical reason.

[study README](./results/io_buf_state_continuous_retrigger_2026-06-20/README.md)

The core failure is this: using one artificial `PSTATE` and mapping it into `KRARG = PSTATE * rise_duration` and `KFARG = (1 - PSTATE) * fall_duration` is not a valid model of HSPICE’s IBIS switching behavior. It samples the wrong parts of the rising/falling coefficient tables during interrupted edges.

Important numbers:

- `short_pulse_1ns_high`: pad RMSE improves, but `Kd` RMSE gets worse: legacy `0.504`, state-continuous `0.635`.
- `short_pulse_2ns_high`: `Kd` RMSE gets much worse: legacy `0.232`, state-continuous `0.684`.
- `double_toggle_1ps`: hard regression, pad RMSE goes from `5.7 mV` to `475.7 mV`.

So the conclusion is: park this algorithm. The next version should fit/emulate HSPICE `Ku/Kd` trajectories directly, with coefficient agreement as the hard gate and pad waveform only as secondary validation.

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

Yes. The previous algorithm failed because it used the wrong state variable.

I tried to make one normalized progress state:

```text
PSTATE = 0 means settled low
PSTATE = 1 means settled high
```

Then I used:

```text
rising table argument  = PSTATE * rising_duration
falling table argument = (1 - PSTATE) * falling_duration
```

That sounds elegant, but it is physically wrong for IBIS switching coefficients.

**What Went Wrong**
For `short_pulse_1ns_high`, the input does this:

```text
5.000 ns: input rises
6.000 ns: input falls again
```

The output has not settled. In fact, because the buffer has delay and finite switching dynamics, HSPICE does not immediately produce a full high output. It produces only a small partial pulse.

What HSPICE does approximately:

```text
before 5 ns:
  Ku ~= 0
  Kd ~= 1
  pad ~= 0 V

after input rises:
  Ku starts to rise only a little
  Kd later turns off briefly
  pad makes a small partial upward pulse

after input falls at 6 ns:
  the rising event is not simply erased
  the falling event does not assume the output was fully high
  Ku stays partial
  Kd recovers
  pad returns low
```

For the 1 ns short pulse, HSPICE showed:

```text
HSPICE Ku peak ~= 0.075
HSPICE pad peak ~= 0.06 V
```

Legacy pybis did this wrong:

```text
new falling edge arrives
restart falling waveform as if previous rise had completed
Ku behaves near full-on
Kd behaves near full-off
pad falsely rises to ~1.5 V
```

My state-continuous algorithm did the opposite wrong thing:

```text
PSTATE only reached ~0.17 by the falling edge
falling table argument = (1 - 0.17) * duration ~= near end of falling table
so Kd target stayed near 1
Ku target stayed near 0
pad stayed near 0
```

That made pad RMSE look much better, but for the wrong reason. It suppressed the driver instead of matching HSPICE.

The giveaway is `Kd`:

```text
short_pulse_1ns_high:
  legacy Kd RMSE ~= 0.504
  state-continuous Kd RMSE ~= 0.635
```

So the coefficient behavior got worse even though the pad waveform looked smaller.

**The Real Issue**
IBIS `Ku/Kd` are not just a normalized “how far through the transition are we?” variable.

They are two independent switching coefficients derived from waveform behavior. They can:

- move at different times
- have different delays
- overshoot slightly
- go slightly negative
- respond to a previous event after the input has already reversed
- have discontinuous-looking slope changes
- partially cancel during short pulses

So one `PSTATE` cannot represent both `Ku` and `Kd`.

The biggest conceptual miss was this:

```text
A short input pulse is not equivalent to:
"start rising, then immediately run falling from the matching progress point."
```

It is closer to:

```text
"launch a delayed rising response, then launch a delayed falling response;
the two coefficient responses overlap/cancel."
```

That distinction matters a lot.

**Correct Direction**
A better model should make `Ku` and `Kd` themselves the state variables.

Not:

```text
PSTATE -> lookup Ku/Kd
```

But:

```text
Ku(t), Kd(t) are continuous state variables
input edges inject/retarget coefficient responses
```

A plausible correct structure is:

```text
on rising input edge:
  schedule/start a rising coefficient response

on falling input edge:
  schedule/start a falling coefficient response

Ku = current Ku plus active rising/falling contributions
Kd = current Kd plus active rising/falling contributions
```

For the 1 ns short pulse, this would mean:

```text
5.000 ns rise edge:
  rising response is launched, but because of delay it has barely affected output by 6 ns

6.000 ns fall edge:
  falling response is launched
  previous rising response is not erased
  overlapping responses create a small partial Ku bump and a temporary Kd drop

result:
  Ku peaks small
  Kd briefly turns off, then recovers
  pad produces small partial pulse
```

That matches the shape HSPICE shows.

**Discontinuity Handling**
We also need to be careful about discontinuities.

Bad behavior:

```text
at input edge:
  Ku jumps from 0 to 1
  Kd jumps from 1 to 0
```

That creates false current injection and can also cause ngspice timestep failures.

Correct behavior:

```text
input logic may jump
event selector may change instantly
but Ku and Kd should usually remain continuous
their derivatives may change sharply
```

So in SPICE terms, `Ku` and `Kd` should probably be capacitor-backed state nodes or smoothed behavioral states, not pure algebraic table switches. A small smoothing time constant is fine, but it must smooth the correct state evolution; smoothing the wrong `PSTATE` just hides the error.

Also, we should not hard-clip away real IBIS behavior. HSPICE coefficients can show small overshoot or slight negative values. The model should allow modest table-derived overshoot, while still guarding against nonphysical blow-up.

**What The Next Algorithm Should Do**
I think the next serious attempt should be one of these two:

1. **Event-response superposition model**

   Treat each input edge as launching a coefficient response kernel:

   ```text
   rising edge:
     add +Ku_rise_kernel(t)
     add -Kd_rise_kernel(t)

   falling edge:
     add -Ku_fall_kernel(t)
     add +Kd_fall_kernel(t)
   ```

   Short pulses naturally become overlapping kernels. This is likely the cleanest explanation and easiest to debug.
2. **Two-state coefficient ODE model**

   Use actual states:

   ```text
   dKu/dt = f(edge, Ku, Kd)
   dKd/dt = g(edge, Ku, Kd)
   ```

   A new edge changes the derivative/target, but does not reset the state. This may be more stable in ngspice but harder to fit.

Either way, the hard validation gate should be:

```text
Ku/Kd must match HSPICE first.
Pad waveform match alone is not enough.
```

The previous algorithm taught us something useful, but mostly by failing clearly: a single progress variable is the wrong abstraction for interrupted IBIS switching.

> # Correct pybis Interrupted-Switching Algorithm Plan
>
> ## Summary
>
> Replace the failed single-`PSTATE` retrigger idea with an independent coefficient-state model. The new model must treat `Ku` and `Kd` as the actual dynamic states, preserve continuity across interrupted edges, and validate against HSPICE using coefficient agreement as the primary gate. Pad-voltage RMSE alone must never be accepted as proof of correctness.
>
> The target behavior for `short_pulse_1ns_high` is:
>
> - input rises at `5 ns`, falls at `6 ns`
> - HSPICE does not produce a full high output
> - `Ku` only makes a small partial bump
> - `Kd` turns off briefly after the delayed rising response, then recovers
> - pad produces a small partial pulse, not a full pulse and not a fake zero-drive result
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Add a new experimental pybis mode named `InputDrivenCoeffState`; leave legacy `InputDriven` unchanged and do not promote the failed `InputDrivenStateContinuous`.
> - Generate independent continuous states for `Ku` and `Kd`; remove the idea that one `PSTATE` can map into both rising and falling tables.
> - Fit coefficient-state dynamics from the IBIS-derived `Ku/Kd` rise/fall tables:
>   - `Ku` and `Kd` each get their own delayed target signal.
>   - Each coefficient uses a small fixed global branch basis, such as delayed first-order branches with separate charge/discharge time constants.
>   - The fit source is only the IBIS/pybis coefficient tables, not HSPICE.
> - Implement coefficient continuity in ngspice:
>   - raw input threshold may switch instantly
>   - delayed target controls may switch instantly
>   - `Ku` and `Kd` themselves must be capacitor-backed state nodes, so they remain continuous
>   - derivative changes are allowed; coefficient jumps are not
> - Use transport-delayed coefficient targets rather than elapsed-time restart:
>   - for a 1 ns pulse, delayed “go high” still arrives after the input has already fallen
>   - `Ku` rises only partially
>   - `Kd` briefly drops, then recovers after the delayed falling command
> - Do not hard-clip coefficients in the normal path. Allow small IBIS-like overshoot/undershoot, but report any coefficient leaving a global sanity range such as `[-0.2, 1.2]`.
> - Expose diagnostic nodes:
>   - `Ku`, `Kd`
>   - `KUTARGET`, `KDTARGET`
>   - optional branch/state nodes for debug plots
> - Update the switching-coefficient sweep to compare three flows:
>   - HSPICE native IBIS
>   - ngspice legacy `InputDriven`
>   - ngspice new `InputDrivenCoeffState`
>
> ## Algorithm Details
>
> - For each coefficient, derive low/high endpoint behavior from the existing coefficient tables:
>   - `Ku_low ~= 0`, `Ku_high ~= 1`
>   - `Kd_low ~= 1`, `Kd_high ~= 0`
> - Fit rise and fall behavior separately for `Ku` and `Kd`:
>   - `Ku` rise: delayed charge toward high
>   - `Ku` fall: delayed discharge toward low
>   - `Kd` rise-edge response: delayed discharge toward low
>   - `Kd` fall-edge response: delayed charge toward high
> - The SPICE structure should be state-based, not table-restart-based:
>   - delayed digital target drives state branches
>   - branches follow the target through fitted time constants
>   - final `Ku/Kd` are weighted sums of continuous branch states
> - Example for `short_pulse_1ns_high`:
>   - `5 ns`: input rises, but coefficient response is delayed
>   - `6 ns`: input falls before output settles
>   - delayed rising response still briefly turns `Kd` off and nudges `Ku` up
>   - delayed falling response then restores `Kd` and removes `Ku`
>   - previous event is not erased, and the falling event does not assume a fully settled high state
>
> ## Validation And Reports
>
> - Extend the existing result folder style with a new canonical output:
>   - `results/io_buf_coeff_state_retrigger_2026-06-20`
> - Metrics must include:
>   - pad RMSE/max error
>   - `Ku` RMSE/max error
>   - `Kd` RMSE/max error
>   - `Ku/Kd` peak values during interrupted pulses
>   - coefficient discontinuity checks
>   - normal-edge regression deltas versus legacy pybis
> - Required cases:
>   - complete edges: `1ps`, `5ps`, `50ps`, `500ps`, `2ns`
>   - load cases: `25R`, `50R`, `100R`, `0pF`, `2pF`, `10pF`
>   - interrupted cases: `500ps`, `1ns`, `2ns` short high pulse
>   - `double_toggle_1ps`
> - Figures must clearly show:
>   - input command
>   - pad waveform overlay
>   - `Ku/Kd` overlay
>   - coefficient target/state diagnostics
>   - pass/fail summary where coefficient metrics are not hidden by pad metrics
>
> ## Acceptance Criteria
>
> - Normal complete-edge cases must not regress:
>   - pad RMSE no worse than legacy by more than `+5 mV`
>   - `Ku/Kd` RMSE no worse than legacy by more than `+0.02`
> - Interrupted short-pulse cases must improve for the right reason:
>   - both `Ku` and `Kd` RMSE improve versus legacy, or any exception is explicitly marked
>   - pad RMSE improves without coefficient false-pass behavior
>   - `Kd` must not stay near `1` when HSPICE turns it off
>   - `Ku` must not jump near full-on for a short partial pulse
> - `double_toggle_1ps` must not show the large state-continuous regression.
> - Any model with coefficient discontinuities, ngspice timestep failures, nonfinite values, or pad-only false pass remains experimental and cannot become default.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - v1 targets push-pull `io_buf`; open-drain can remain legacy until this method is proven.
> - HSPICE is validation only; the new generated model must be derived from IBIS/pybis coefficient tables.
> - The failed `InputDrivenStateContinuous` mode should be preserved only as a negative comparison or removed from normal documentation.
> - The new default remains legacy `InputDriven` until `InputDrivenCoeffState` passes the full coefficient-first validation sweep.

</details>

Implemented the new experimental `InputDrivenCoeffState` path and ran the full coefficient-first validation sweep.

**What changed**

- Added `InputDrivenCoeffState` to [subcircuit.py](./tools/pybis2spice/pybis2spice/subcircuit.py).
- Legacy `InputDriven` is unchanged.
- The new mode uses independent Ku/Kd continuous branch states derived from IBIS/pybis coefficient tables.
- Added diagnostics: `Ku`, `Kd`, `KUTARGET`, `KDTARGET`.
- Added the sweep runner: [run_io_buf_coeff_state_retrigger.py](./scripts/run_io_buf_coeff_state_retrigger.py).
- Added generation tests in [test_pybis2spice.py](./tools/pybis2spice/test/test_pybis2spice.py).

**Validation output**
Report:
[README.md](./results/io_buf_coeff_state_retrigger_2026-06-20/README.md)

Plots:
[plots/cases](./results/io_buf_coeff_state_retrigger_2026-06-20/plots/cases)

Key files:

- `metrics_by_case.csv`
- `legacy_vs_coeff_state_summary.csv`
- `common/legacy/driver_OutputInput_Typical.sub`
- `common/coeff_state/driver_OutputInput_Typical.sub`

**Result**
The new algorithm is useful, but not default-ready.

It improves interrupted short pulses:

- `short_pulse_2ns_high`: pad RMSE `361 mV -> 204 mV`
- `short_pulse_1ns_high`: pad RMSE `653 mV -> 98 mV`
- `short_pulse_500ps_high`: pad RMSE `679 mV -> 48 mV`

It also keeps Ku partial instead of letting it jump near full-on like legacy pybis.

But it regresses normal complete edges:

- `9` complete-edge regressions out of `10`
- Example `edge_1ps_base_50r_2pf`: legacy pad RMSE `5.3 mV`, coeff-state `150.7 mV`

So the conclusion is: this branch-state direction fixes the right short-pulse failure mechanism, but it cannot replace legacy `InputDriven` yet because complete edges get worse.

**Verified**

- Full HSPICE/native IBIS vs ngspice legacy vs ngspice coeff-state sweep completed: `13 / 13` cases.
- Targeted pybis2spice tests passed: `2 / 2`.
- Python compile checks passed.

Next best step: make this a hybrid mode, where legacy remains active for normal complete edges and the coefficient-state path only takes over when an interrupted/retriggered transition is detected.

I focused the case study on `short_pulse_1ns_high`.

Main finding:

- HSPICE Ku peak: `0.075`
- Legacy pybis Ku peak: `1.013`
- CoeffState Ku peak: `0.361`

So the new algorithm does fix the worst legacy failure: it no longer lets Ku go fully on for a 1 ns interrupted pulse. The pad also improves a lot:

- HSPICE pad peak: `0.062 V`
- Legacy pad peak: `1.516 V`
- CoeffState pad peak: `0.219 V`

But it is still not correct enough: CoeffState Ku is still too high versus HSPICE, and Kd recovers too smoothly instead of matching HSPICE’s sharper dip/recovery. The control-vs-interrupted figure also makes the tradeoff clear: this helps interrupted pulses but regresses normal complete edges, so the next algorithm should be hybrid/event-aware rather than replacing legacy behavior globally.

>
> ## Summary
>
> Continue from the current `InputDrivenCoeffState` result by building a short-pulse-focused hybrid experiment. The goal is not to replace legacy pybis globally. The goal is to prove whether we can improve interrupted short-pulse behavior while leaving normal long-pulse behavior unchanged.

> ## Key Changes
>
> - Add a new experimental pybis mode, separate from legacy:
>
>   - Name: `InputDrivenShortPulseHybrid`
>   - Legacy `InputDriven` remains unchanged and remains default.
>   - Existing `InputDrivenCoeffState` remains available as a comparison baseline, not promoted.
> - Keep normal behavior untouched:
>
>   - In default runs, legacy pybis must behave exactly as it does today.

>     - `short_pulse_2ns_high`
>     - `edge_1ps_base_50r_2pf` as the normal long-pulse control.
> - Hybrid algorithm direction:
>
>   - Generate both legacy coefficient logic and short-pulse correction logic inside the experimental subcircuit.
>   - Detect short high pulses only when the input falls before a global IBIS-derived retrigger window has expired.
>   - When no short-pulse condition is active, use legacy `Ku/Kd`.
>   - When short-pulse condition is active, use capacitor-backed continuous correction states so `Ku/Kd` do not jump.
>   - Derive correction timing from IBIS/pybis coefficient tables only; HSPICE is validation, not fitting input.
>   - Candidate delay estimators to evaluate globally:
>     - current branch-state onset
